items.label: text
items.text: If we carry out electrolysis of molten sodium chloride, we get sodium at the cathode (negative electrode) and chlorine at the anode (positive electrode). The ionic half-equations are:

items.label: text
items.text: cathode:Na+ + e⁻ → Na reduction

items.label: text
items.text: Sodium ions are reduced to sodium atoms.

items.label: text
items.text: anode:

items.label: formula
items.text: 2 C I \rightarrow C I _ { 2 } + 2 e ^ { - }

items.label: text
items.text: oxidation

items.label: text
items.text: Chloride ions are oxidised to chlorine molecules.

items.label: text
items.text: These half-equations must always balance in terms of the number of atoms on each side, but also in terms of the charges; the total charge must be the same on both sides. This is why we need 2 electrons in the second half-equation but only 1 in the first.

items.label: text
items.text: Let us look at another example, the electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide (Al2O3). We get aluminium at the cathode and oxygen at the anode. Aluminium is in Group 3 in the Periodic Table and so an aluminium atom has 3 electrons in its outer shell. You may remember from Chapter 7 that this means that Al forms a 3+ ion. This 3+ ion will be attracted to the negative electrode in electrolysis and we will get the reaction:

items.label: formula
items.text: A | ^ { 3 + } + 3 e ^ { - } \rightarrow A |

items.label: text
items.text: In order to cancel out the 3+ charge on the Al³+ ion we need to add 3 electrons. The total charge on the left-hand side is zero (3+ + 3-), which is the same as on the right-hand side. Another way to think about this is that if an aluminium atom loses 3 electrons to form an Al³+ ion, we must put those electrons backin order to form the atom again. This is a reduction reaction because the Al³+ ion gains electrons.

items.label: text
items.text: When we electrolyse molten aluminium oxide, the half-equation for the reaction at the anode is:

items.label: text
items.text: Each O²- ion has 2 'extra' electrons and oxygen atoms go around in pairs, so we must remove 4 electrons to form O2. These are shown on the right-hand side of the half-equation. There are two Os on each side and the total charge on each side is 4-. This is an oxidation reaction.

items.label: text
items.text: When molten zinc(ll) chloride is electrolysed, zinc is obtained at the cathode and chlorine at the anode:

items.label: text
items.text: cathode: Zn²+ + 2e- → Zn reduction

items.label: text
items.text: anode:

items.label: text
items.text: 2Cl- → Cl2}+ 2e− oxidation

items.label: text
items.text: We can make the following generalisations from the reactions above:

items.label: list_item
items.text: If you electrolyse a molten ionic compound only containing two elements, you will get the metal at the cathode (because metals form positive ions) and the non-metal at the anode (because non-metals form negative ions).

items.label: list_item
items.text: Reduction always occurs at the cathode and oxidation always occurs at the anode.

items.label: text
items.text: You can probably see now that positive ions are known as cations because they are attracted to the cathode (negative electrode). Negative ions are known as anions because they are attracted to the anode (positive electrode).
